demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette: Daniel is a 34-year-old school counselor who came to treatment nearly a year after a car accident in which he struck a teenage pedestrian outside a medical office complex near his school district. He had been driving home after a long, tense day, distracted and keyed up, when the boy stepped off the curb between parked cars. Daniel still remembers the sweet chemical smell drifting from the clinic's open doorway, the flash of a white exam-paper gown through the glass, and the sickening thud that followed before he had fully understood what he had done. The boy survived but was seriously injured. Daniel can say the facts in fragments, but whenever he tries to tell the story in order, the words disappear. What comes back instead is not a narrative but a total reliving: the smell, the sight of the body on the pavement, the sound of shouting, all of it arriving as if it is happening now. In the weeks after the accident, everyday strain began to feel dangerous to him. A hard day at school, a parent conflict, even the pressured noise of students moving through the hallway could make him feel as if he were back in the seconds before impact. Because he had come to see himself as someone who failed under pressure, stress no longer registered as ordinary strain; it snagged his attention as evidence, and that made crowded hallways, sharp voices, and rushed moments far more likely to set off reminders of the accident. Medical settings became especially potent. If he had to accompany a student to the nurse's office, or if he passed the district clinic and caught the disinfectant smell, his body reacted immediately; his chest tightened, his skin went cold, and the scene returned in full sensory detail. In those moments he was flooded not only with the accident itself but with the conviction that it had happened because of the way he acted. The conviction was not separate from the reliving; telling himself that he was the kind of man who could do this made the memory easier to reach and harsher when it came, as if the scene kept returning to prove what he believed about himself. He had come to believe that he could not trust himself to do the right thing under pressure, and each trigger seemed to prove it again. That belief hardened over time into something broader and more devastating. Daniel was certain that his life had been destroyed by what he had done. He no longer saw himself as a careful, dependable person but as someone fundamentally unsafe, the kind of man who could ruin another family in a single careless moment. Because he viewed his own judgment as untrustworthy, he worked constantly to keep his mind occupied: podcasts in the car, grading or email late into the evening, television on in the background, anything to prevent a quiet moment in which the accident might come back. He also went out of his way to avoid police cars, officers at school events, or even news stories about investigations, because contact with police immediately pulled him toward the thought that he should have been punished more harshly. Needing this much distraction and detouring became its own kind of proof to him that he was not steady anymore; every workaround quietly confirmed his fear that he could not cope like other people and that something fundamental in him had been damaged. He tried not to think about the event at all, yet the effort itself seemed to keep it close, and afterward he felt even more ashamed that he was still living this way. The avoidance had also spread the accident across his daily map: the clinic he skirted, the officers he watched for, the stories he skipped all became reminders in their own right, so that more and more of ordinary life carried the outline of what had happened. At work this pattern has become woven into his days. As a counselor he is often the adult students come to when they are distressed, but heightened stress in his office now makes him scan himself and the room as if some fresh catastrophe is about to happen. That same keyed-up sense of imminent disaster kept the accident close by in his mind; once he was on alert, the memory was much harder to hold off and could break through with very little warning. When the sense of danger rose that quickly, stepping back, keeping busy, and finding a reason to leave felt like the only practical way to get through the moment without being overwhelmed. If a student has a panic attack and the nurse is called, Daniel finds reasons to step into the hall rather than stay near the cot, the latex gloves, the alcohol wipes. He tells himself he is giving staff space, though he knows he is escaping the smell and the medical routine that can make the accident burst back with such force. Because he almost never stayed long enough to learn that these moments could pass safely, his body kept treating them as genuinely dangerous, and the threat in medical situations remained as sharp as ever. The more he avoids these situations, the less confidence he has in his ability to handle them, and that loss of confidence sharpens his sense that he is damaged beyond repair. Nights are often the worst. Daniel has difficulty falling asleep because he feels he needs to stay alert, as if relaxing would leave him unguarded against the memory. In bed, any rise in tension can become its own trigger; once he notices his body is keyed up, he braces for the accident to return, and it often does. When the memory surges, it arrives with such immediacy that he feels he is again at the wheel, smelling antiseptic and hearing the impact, and the terror and guilt hit his body at full strength. Afterward he lies awake monitoring every sound in the house, ashamed and angry with himself for not being able to control his own mind. Each time that happened, the thought that followed was painfully familiar: if the accident could still take over his mind like this, then maybe he really was as unsafe and permanently altered as he feared. To avoid that spiral he scrolls on his phone, watches videos, or mentally jumps to tomorrow's tasks, but the exhaustion leaves him more stressed the next day, more reactive, and more vulnerable to the same intrusions. By the time he sought help, Daniel's world had narrowed around these efforts to prevent remembering. His wife had begun telling him that even when he was home, he seemed elsewhere, always busy, unreachable, tense. What finally brought him in was a routine physical for himself: sitting in an exam room on crinkling paper, breathing in the smell of disinfectant, he felt the accident engulf him so completely that he had to leave before the doctor came in. He was shaken not only by the reliving but by what it seemed to confirm-that he could not trust himself, that one event had ruined his life, and that he might never again be the steady person his students and family believed him to be. What he hopes for now, cautiously, is not to forget, but to find a way for the memory to become past instead of something he has to survive over and over. And once the memory had broken through in the night, the next day was full of fresh points of contact with it; ordinary tension, a slammed door, even the smell of cleaning products seemed more charged, as though the reliving had taught his attention to keep finding pieces of the accident everywhere.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not clearly state that Daniel’s negative appraisals directly cause or intensify the trauma memory.
The vignette does not clearly convey that Daniel’s negative beliefs lead him to experience more triggers or reminders.
The vignette does not explicitly show the trauma memory leading to or strengthening Daniel’s negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
The vignette does not explicitly describe the trauma memory causing triggers or reminders to arise.
The vignette does not clearly state that Daniel’s sense of threat directly leads to avoidance or other maladaptive strategies.
The vignette does not explicitly show Daniel’s perceived threat causing the trauma memory to return.
The vignette does not clearly convey that Daniel’s avoidance or other maladaptive strategies directly strengthen his negative appraisals.
The vignette does not explicitly describe maladaptive strategies leading to increased triggers or reminders.
The vignette does not clearly state that Daniel’s maladaptive strategies contribute to an increased sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette does not clearly state that Daniel’s negative appraisals directly cause or intensify the trauma memory.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly convey that Daniel’s negative beliefs lead him to experience more triggers or reminders.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not explicitly show the trauma memory leading to or strengthening Daniel’s negative appraisals within the same paragraph.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly describe the trauma memory causing triggers or reminders to arise.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not clearly state that Daniel’s sense of threat directly leads to avoidance or other maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "When the threat felt this close, planning her exit from every room she entered wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible."
  e.g. "She had found that checking the locks twice was the only thing that allowed her body to settle enough to sleep, so she checked them twice."
  e.g. "The only way to move through the world at that level of fear was to make it smaller — fewer places, fewer people, fewer chances for something to go wrong."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not explicitly show Daniel’s perceived threat causing the trauma memory to return.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not clearly convey that Daniel’s avoidance or other maladaptive strategies directly strengthen his negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly describe maladaptive strategies leading to increased triggers or reminders.
  e.g. "Each place she avoided became a reminder in itself — the long way round she walked every morning was its own daily acknowledgement of what had happened."
  e.g. "Her safety behaviours had drawn a map of the event around her: everything she couldn't do, everywhere she couldn't go, every person she kept at arm's length."
  e.g. "The avoidance had grown in all directions until the city was full of routes she no longer used and things she could no longer say."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not clearly state that Daniel’s maladaptive strategies contribute to an increased sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
